newsitem.title: USA: Do real men eat quiche? They DO use coupons.
newsitem.headline: Do real men eat quiche? They DO use coupons.

text.p: One of the hottest debates some years ago was whether real men eat quiche. While the answer is still up in the air, one thing is certain. Real men DO use coupons.

"Thirty percent of all men who go grocery shopping won't go shopping without coupons," said Paul Wilson, a self-described student of the supermarket industry and inventor, citing industry statistics. Coupons are also used by 35 percent of all women who grocery shop.
Men, as a rule, use more coupons per visit than women, he said. No reason has been given, but Wilson said the money-saving aspect of supermarket coupons is appreciated by all, regardless of gender.
"Even using coupons as a nominal exercise, say six a week, that's a savings of $200 a year," he said, given that the average coupon is worth 67 cents.
"The average family of four can save 20 percent of annual grocery bills -- saving over $1,000 -- by using coupons regularly and consistently," he said.
Currently, only 2 percent of all coupons in circulation are redeemed, but 82 percent of all households use coupons at one time or another, he said.

A resident of Escondido, Calif., Wilson has spent much of his adult life in and around supermarkets. He studied marketing at the University of Southern California and has held various positions at supermarket companies.

An advocate of coupons both in his personal and professional lives, Wilson said that while you might be accruing value for your shopping dollars, nothing comes without some strings attached. He cautioned there are some definite dos and don'ts when it comes to using coupons.
Coupons can not be traded from one consumer to another. Clearly written on coupons are the words "non-transferrable."
"As long as you buy the newspaper that has the coupon, you're OK. Your aunt in Pittsburgh can't send you a coupon that's worth more."
Trading coupons is "a gray area" of legality, he said.
However, if you buy the newspaper, the coupon is yours, regardless of where the newspaper was purchased.

"When you see, in your own paper or on a trip, a particularly valuable coupon you will definitely use, weigh the savings against the extra cost of another newspaper or two and clip a few extras," he writes in a booklet, "Real Men Use Coupons, Too!"

Knowing the manufacturer's game is one of the "insider" secrets that Wilson shares in the booklet. He writes that while coupon values differ dramatically by region, or stores might double or triple the coupon's value, "What they don't tell you is they're in cahoots with the manufacturers.
"Coupons distributed in those regions are typically worth only 40 to 50 percent of the ones your relatives in another part of the country are clipping.
"Double those anaemic coupons and the supermarket and manufacturer still put a big one over on you."
Don't be fooled, he said. The rumours of coupons' demise is greatly exaggerated.

They've been around for 101 years, introduced by Coca-Cola in 1896, offering a discount at a local soda fountain. While some manufacturers may treaten to discontinue coupons, such as a recent experiment by Procter & Gamble Co. in three counties in New York state, what the threats actually do is prompt even more people to use coupons.
"No manufacturer dares to drop coupons in too big an area or for too long a time. First, consumers are too used to taking advantage of the savings.

"Second, competitors are quick to seize the opportunity and flood us with coupons of their own. ... Next time you see a coupon cutback story, listen very carefully. That sound you hear is kitchen drawers and scissors all over town in a frenzied last blast of couponing!" he writes.

A few years back, Wilson said, 90 percent of coupons redeemed came from Sunday newspaper ad supplements. Today, newspapers account for only 70 percent to 75 percent of those coupons redeemed. Consumers need to look for coupons in packages, on packages and in the supermarkets themselves.

Reasons for coupon distribution have also changed, with manufacturers now using them as a way to keep customers loyal to the brand, rather than a way to introduce consumers to a particular product. Thus, if a consumer calls an 800- number on a package or writes to the company, chances are she'll receive coupons from the company as a bonus.

To get the most out of coupons, Wilson advises keeping coupons with you all the time -- thus the idea behind his patented product. He has invented a revolving index wheel that saves and catalogues clipped coupons, the Coup-o-Dex. It is designed to fit over the handles of a supermarket shopping cart and contains a calculator.
